task_brief: Day 2 of "Object-Oriented and Modular Design" (unit 2, grade 11) is a worked-model trace on encapsulation and interfaces. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Refactor a procedural program into a modular design and demonstrate preserved behavior with tests. Today's work contributes to that by handling encapsulation and interfaces at the explicit model stage, against the unit's wider topics of objects classes and state, encapsulation and interfaces, composition and inheritance tradeoffs, and modules and dependencies. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Work through the provided worked model of encapsulation and interfaces one step at a time rather than reading it straight through. For each step, write what changed and why that step is legal. Build a trace table with one row per step showing the values or states before and after. Then change exactly one line, value, or condition in the model, predict the new result before running or re-tracing it, and record whether your prediction was right. Explain in your own words the rule that makes encapsulation and interfaces behave the way the model shows. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about encapsulation and interfaces, and it belongs to "Object-Oriented and Modular Design", which also covers separate topics such as objects classes and state. Close out with this check before you stop: Explain the modelled approach to encapsulation and interfaces in your own words and name the step most likely to go wrong. At grade 11 the bar is independent work with sustained self-direction: you set the constraint, defend it, and revise on the evidence of your own checks rather than on being told to.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Any model, source, or artifact under study is supplied in an accessible parallel form: text alternative or transcript, described version, and a tactile or enlarged rendering where the original is visual. The learner is never required to perceive the source in one specific channel to analyse it.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.

remediation: Reteaching for encapsulation and interfaces follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for encapsulation and interfaces, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to encapsulation and interfaces works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of encapsulation and interfaces, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking encapsulation and interfaces mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply encapsulation and interfaces under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on encapsulation and interfaces rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
